_meta.purpose: Citation graph for the Pit Log content spine. Every factual record in content/ points at an id here. Nothing in this file was written from memory: every url was fetched and read on the accessed date.

tiers.3: recognised industry body or standards organisation
tiers.5: credible practitioner reporting. QUALITATIVE ONLY. May never carry a safety claim.

update_sensitivity.safety-critical: revised guidance changes what is SAFE. Recheck on any change.
update_sensitivity.volatile: moves with markets, catalogues or programme terms. Recheck on a cadence.
update_sensitivity.stable: physics, anatomy, published standards. Changes rarely.

_meta.fetch_note: fsis.usda.gov, beefitswhatsfordinner.com, alaskaseafood.org and gelato.com return HTTP 403 to non-browser user agents. Read them through a real browser session; the 403 is bot filtering, not a dead page.

sources.org: USDA Food Safety and Inspection Service
sources.title: Safe Minimum Internal Temperature Chart
supports: Beef, pork, veal and lamb steaks, chops and roasts: 145 F (62.8 C) and rest at least 3 minutes
Ground meats: 160 F (71.1 C)
All poultry, including ground poultry, giblets and stuffing: 165 F (73.9 C)
Ham, fresh or smoked (uncooked): 145 F and rest at least 3 minutes
Fully cooked ham to reheat: 140 F if packaged in a USDA-inspected plant, otherwise 165 F
Fish and shellfish: 145 F (62.8 C)
Eggs: 160 F. Leftovers and casseroles: 165 F
Measured with a food thermometer before removing food from the heat source
For reasons of personal preference, consumers may choose to cook food to higher temperatures

sources.org: USDA Food Safety and Inspection Service
sources.title: Beef From Farm to Table
supports: Four basic major primal cuts of beef: chuck, loin, rib and round
Chuck and round are less tender and require moist heat; loin and rib can be cooked by dry heat
Retail names vary regionally: a boneless top loin steak is also strip steak, Kansas City steak, N.Y. strip steak
Ground beef and organ meats to 160 F; steaks and roasts to 145 F with a 3 minute rest
Never brown or partially cook beef to finish later
Marinate in the refrigerator up to 5 days; boil used marinade before brushing on cooked beef
It is safe to cook frozen beef without defrosting; time is about 50% longer. Do not cook frozen beef in a slow cooker
Refrigerate cooked beef within 2 hours (1 hour above 90 F); use within 3 to 4 days or reheat to 165 F
Chuck roast and brisket: braise at 325 F, 1.5 to 2.5 hours for 3 to 4 lb (planning table only)

sources.org: USDA Food Safety and Inspection Service
sources.title: Fresh Pork From Farm to Table
supports: Four basic primal cuts of pork: shoulder, loin, side and leg
Shoulder yields shoulder butt roast or steak, blade steak, boneless blade Boston roast, arm picnic, hock, ground pork
Side yields spareribs, back ribs and bacon
Loin yields whole loin, loin roast, tenderloin, sirloin roast, country style ribs, chops
Leg yields ham, fresh or smoked and cured
Pork steaks, chops and roasts to 145 F with a 3 minute rest; ground pork and organ meats to 160 F
Cooked muscle meats can be pink even at a safe internal temperature; fresh pork at 145 F throughout is safe even if pink
Trichinella is destroyed at 145 F with the 3 minute rest
Boston butt roasting at 350 F: about 45 minutes per pound (planning table only, compiled from various resources)
Ribs, all types, 1.5 to 2 hours or until fork tender (planning table only)

sources.org: USDA Food Safety and Inspection Service
sources.title: Lamb From Farm to Table
supports: Five basic major primal cuts of lamb: shoulder, rack, shank/breast, loin and leg
The rack is the rib primal and contains 9 full ribs
Loin chops and rib chops are the most tender and most expensive; blade and arm chops (shoulder) and sirloin chops (leg) are less expensive but may be just as tender
Lamb steaks, chops and roasts to 145 F with a 3 minute rest; ground lamb and organ meats to 160 F
Lamb is produced from animals typically under a year old; mutton from older animals
Shanks and breast: braise or simmer 1.5 to 2 hours (planning table only)

sources.org: USDA Food Safety and Inspection Service
sources.title: Chicken from Farm to Table
supports: Whole chicken to 165 F, checked in the innermost part of the thigh and wing and the thickest part of the breast
All poultry to 165 F; consumers may choose higher for personal preference
The colour of cooked chicken is not a sign of its safety; pink can persist at 165 F, and smoking or grilling makes it more likely, especially in young birds
Do not pre-stuff a bird to cook later; stuff immediately before cooking; frozen stuffed poultry must be cooked from frozen
Washing raw poultry is not recommended; it spreads bacteria
Do not cook frozen chicken in a slow cooker or microwave; oven or stove is fine at about 50% longer
Refrigerate cooked chicken within 2 hours; use within 3 to 4 days or reheat to 165 F

Grilling planning times: breast halves bone-in 10 to 15 min per side, boneless 6 to 8; legs or thighs 10 to 15 per side; wings 8 to 12 per side; whole broiler-fryer 60 to 75 min indirect (planning table only)

sources.org: USDA Food Safety and Inspection Service
sources.title: Goat From Farm to Table
supports: Retail cuts of goat are similar to those for lamb or mutton
Goat steaks, chops and roasts to 145 F with a 3 minute rest; ground goat to 160 F
A goat carcass rarely has much fat to protect it from drying; goat meat is generally quite lean
Less tender cuts should be braised or stewed; kid lends itself to all lamb recipes
Goat is classified as red meat

sources.org: USDA Food Safety and Inspection Service
sources.title: Smoking Meat and Poultry
supports: Use two thermometers: one for the smoker air, one for the food
Smoker air temperature should stay between 225 and 300 F throughout the cook
Smoking can take 4 to 8 hours; time depends on meat, size, distance from heat, coal temperature and weather
Smoke to the safe minimum internal temperature: 145 F plus 3 minute rest for whole-muscle beef, pork, lamb and veal; 160 F ground; 165 F poultry
Apply sauce in the last 15 to 30 minutes to prevent burning
Refrigerate smoked meat within 2 hours of removing it from the smoker; use within 4 days or freeze
Thaw before smoking. Marinate in the refrigerator. Never partially cook to finish later
Hickory, apple or maple chips give the most satisfactory smoke flavour (FSIS wording)
Do not smoke in makeshift containers such as galvanized cans

sources.org: USDA Food Safety and Inspection Service
sources.title: Doneness Versus Safety
supports: Appearance and colour are not reliable indicators of safety or doneness
Doneness is a sensory state (texture, appearance, juiciness); safety is destruction of harmful bacteria
One in four hamburgers that look done may not be safely cooked
Insert the thermometer into the thickest part, not touching bone, fat or gristle

sources.org: USDA Food Safety and Inspection Service
sources.title: Food Thermometers
supports: A food thermometer is the only reliable way to ensure a safe minimum internal temperature
Place the thermometer in the thickest part, away from bone, fat or gristle; for thin foods insert through the side
Check large or irregular pieces in several places
Read the manufacturer's instructions for insertion depth; the stem dimple marks the sensing area

sources.org: USDA Food Safety and Inspection Service
sources.title: Danger Zone (40 F - 140 F)
supports: Bacteria grow most rapidly between 40 F and 140 F, doubling in as little as 20 minutes
Never leave food out of refrigeration over 2 hours; 1 hour if above 90 F
Keep hot food at or above 140 F; keep cold food at or below 40 F
When roasting meat and poultry, use an oven temperature no lower than 325 F

sources.org: U.S. Food and Drug Administration
sources.title: Selecting and Serving Fresh and Frozen Seafood Safely
supports: Most seafood should be cooked to an internal temperature of 145 F
Cooked fish: the flesh is clear and separates easily with a fork

sources.org: Cattlemen's Beef Board and National Cattlemen's Beef Association (Beef Checkoff)
sources.title: Beef. It's What's For Dinner: Cuts and primal pages
supports: Brisket is a primal cut: the animal's breast, tougher because it is used for movement, ideal for low and slow
Brisket Flat Half is the leaner 'first cut'; Brisket Point Half is the less lean, juicier half
Flat iron steak is cut from the top blade (chuck) and is the second most tender beef cut
Tri-tip roast is boneless, fairly tender, full flavour; roast or grill then slice across the grain
Flank steak is lean and boneless; best marinated and grilled or sliced thin
Chuck short ribs are flavourful, moist and tender when slow-cooked

sources.org: Cattlemen's Beef Board and National Cattlemen's Beef Association (Beef Checkoff)
sources.title: Determining Doneness
supports: Steaks: medium-rare reads 145 F and rest at least three minutes; medium 160 F; well done 170 F (final temperatures)
Insert an instant-read thermometer horizontally from the side into the thickest part, not touching bone or fat
Ground beef to 160 F; colour is not a reliable indicator, and meatloaf may stay pink at 160 F because of natural nitrates in onions, celery and peppers
Roasts: temperature continues to rise 5 to 15 F after removal from the oven; allow 15 to 20 minutes standing time

sources.org: National Pork Board (Pork Checkoff)
sources.title: Pork Cuts
supports: Retail pork cut families: bacon, ground pork, ham, pork belly, pork chops, pork loin roast, pork rib roast, pork ribs, pork shoulder, pork steak, pork tenderloin, sausage
Pork shoulder goes by picnic roast, Boston butt, blade roast and pork butt
Pork belly is the boneless cut that remains after the loin and spareribs are removed

sources.org: National Pork Board (Pork Checkoff)
sources.title: Smoking Pork
supports: Most popular pork cuts to smoke: shoulder, loin, chops, belly, ribs
Loin back ribs 3 to 5 hours at 225-250 F; St. Louis and spareribs 5 to 7 hours at 225-250 F; times vary with thickness
Pork butt / picnic / whole shoulder: about 1 hour 15 minutes per pound; cook to an internal temperature of 185-190 F, the bone will easily slip from the meat
Pork loin: cook to 140 F then rest in a warm place 10 minutes until it reaches 145 F
Pork chops: 145 F followed by a 3 minute rest
Pork belly: 4 hours smoke, wrap, 3 more hours; cook to 190 F or until fork tender

sources.org: American Lamb Board
sources.title: Learn About the Different Cuts of Lamb
supports: Rack of lamb: eight chops per rack, about 2 lb; roast; Frenched or crown roast variations
Lamb shoulder roast: upper front shoulder, tougher with more fat than leg, richer flavour, requires low and slow
Lamb shoulder chops (blade or arm chops) are economical and quick-cooking
Lamb shanks, fore and hind, practically melt off the bone when slow cooked; braise
Boneless leg (BRT) is the leanest and most versatile cut, about 7 to 8 lb whole
Lamb ribs are cost-effective, can substitute for pork ribs; braise and grill
Loin chops are lean and tender with a T-shaped bone

sources.org: American Lamb Board
sources.title: Lamb Cooking Time & Temperature (PDF)
supports: Medium rare: pull at 135 F, final 145 F after a 3 minute rest. Medium: pull 150 F, final 160 F. Well: pull 160 F, final 170 F
Pull lamb from the heat when it is 10 degrees lower than the desired doneness because the internal temperature will rise
Lamb shoulder benefits from slow cooking to break down connective tissue; braise, roast or smoke
Lamb shanks should be braised 1 to 2 hours per lb to medium (160 F)
Always cut against the grain; let lamb rest; use a meat thermometer

sources.org: Texas A&M University, Department of Animal Science, Meat Science Section
sources.title: Texas Barbecue: How to Cook and Smoke Barbecue
supports: Cuts such as briskets and pork butts need low temperatures (200 to 250 F) so the outside does not overcook while the centre comes up
Planning estimate: about one hour of cooking per pound of raw cut for large barbecue cuts
The four primary Texas barbecue woods are hickory, oak, pecan and mesquite
Wood preference is often what people grew up eating; too little smoke is unsatisfying, too much overpowers the meat

sources.org: Texas A&M University, Department of Animal Science, Meat Science Section
sources.title: Texas Barbecue: Barbecue Science
supports: The plateau in internal temperature near the end of cooking is evaporative cooling
Collagen is converted to gelatin when heated; a higher internal temperature, 185 to 195 F, is required to achieve this conversion

Briskets have a high percentage of connective tissue containing collagen; muscle fibre toughens with heat while connective tissue tenderises, which is why brisket is taken to a high internal temperature
The smoke ring is nitric oxide from burning wood combining with myoglobin to form nitrosyl hemochromogen

sources.org: Texas A&M University, Department of Animal Science, Meat Science Section
sources.title: Texas Barbecue: Meat Selection for Barbecuing
supports: Brisket points are the anterior end and typically fatter; flats are considerably leaner in cover and within the muscle
Packer-trimmed briskets keep a thicker fat cover that many enthusiasts prefer for long cooking
Cooked, trimmed lean yield of brisket is approximately 50% of raw weight
Briskets have high levels of connective tissue and require longer cooking at low temperatures
Shoulder clod muscles are inherently more tender than brisket and may not need as high an internal temperature
Back ribs carry large amounts of connective tissue: slow, low, even high-moisture cooking recommended; short ribs require long-time low-heat cookery

sources.org: AmazingRibs.com (Meathead), reporting experiments by Prof. Greg Blonder, Boston University
sources.title: What Causes The BBQ Stall: It's Not What You Think
supports: Controlled-smoker experiment by Prof. Greg Blonder (physicist, Boston University): a water-soaked sponge stalled like a brisket while pure beef fat heated steadily, so the stall is evaporative cooling, not fat rendering
The stall typically begins between 150 and 170 F and can last hours
Wrapping (the Texas crutch) traps humidity, stops evaporative cooling and pushes the cut through the stall
QUALITATIVE ONLY: a practitioner site; it carries no safety claim in this spine
